purpose: Dextrose is a type of simple sugar that is used to treat low blood sugar (hypoglycemia) or to provide energy when you cannot eat. It is also used in IV fluids to give your body calories and keep your energy levels up. Doctors may also use it alongside other medications given through an IV.
how_it_works: Dextrose is basically the same as the natural glucose (sugar) your body uses for energy. When given by mouth or through an IV, it goes straight into your bloodstream and raises your blood sugar levels quickly. Your body's cells then absorb it and use it as fuel to keep your brain, muscles, and organs working properly.
common_side_effects: Swelling or irritation at the injection site if given through an IV, increased urination, feeling flushed or warm, and higher than normal blood sugar levels if too much is given. You may also feel thirsty or have a mild headache.
warnings: If you have diabetes, dextrose can raise your blood sugar too high, so it must be used carefully and monitored closely. Getting too much dextrose can cause fluid overload, which may lead to swelling or breathing problems. Let your doctor or nurse know if you have kidney problems, heart problems, or are on a fluid-restricted diet. Never give the concentrated form (D50W) by mouth — it is only for IV use by medical professionals.
typical_dosing: The dose depends on why you need it and how it is being given. For low blood sugar, a common adult oral dose is 15 to 20 grams (about 3 to 4 glucose tablets or gel). For IV use in a hospital, the dose and concentration are determined by your medical team based on your condition and blood sugar levels. Always follow your healthcare provider's instructions.
